item.title: Small Business Research Programs: Selected Agencies Address Foreign Risks and Take Various Approaches to Track Data
item.description:
What GAO Found
The SBIR and STTR Extension Act of 2022 (Extension Act) requires participating agencies to assess security risks posed by small businesses applying for funding through the Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) and Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) programs. GAO found that the five agencies it examined do so by considering a range of individuals and factors (see figure). For example, to identify risks associated with foreign ownership, agencies may review business investors’ and owners’ foreign connections and debts.
Individuals and Factors Selected Agencies May Consider to Identify and Assess Foreign Risks
In general, selected agencies identify foreign risks using a standardized disclosure form about an applicant’s foreign affiliations and financial support. Agencies then verify disclosures using analytical tools or counterintelligence reviews. After assessing an applicant’s risk level, agencies decide whether to award, mitigate risk by adding certain conditions, or deny the award.
GAO also found that the five selected agencies use various approaches to maintain and track data on their due diligence activities, such as automated systems and spreadsheets. In fiscal years (FY) 2024 and 2025, agencies performed due diligence on over 28,000 SBIR and STTR proposals and identified over 1,700 possible foreign risks (see figure). They also identified over 11,000 other risks, such as risks related to patents or cybersecurity. Examples of foreign risks include a researcher who is currently a professor in China, and a company that did not disclose that it maintained a foreign business entity.
Agency-Reported Foreign Risks, Fiscal Years 2024 and 2025
Why GAO Did This Study
The SBIR and STTR programs fund research and development by U.S. small businesses. In FY2024, federal agencies issued more than 6,400 such awards in areas such as defense, energy, and health care. However, U.S. intelligence agencies have expressed concerns about foreign adversaries seeking to obtain proprietary data from small businesses via these programs, potentially threatening national security.
The Extension Act requires participating agencies to implement due diligence programs to assess the security risks posed by small business applicants. It includes a provision for GAO to issue a series of reports on these due diligence efforts. This report, the fourth in the series, examines (1) how five selected agencies and components—the Air Force, the Department of Energy, the National Institutes of Health, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, and the National Science Foundation—address foreign risks and (2) the extent to which selected agencies collect and track data on these efforts.
To address these objectives, GAO selected the five agencies that issue the most awards annually based on FY2024 data. GAO reviewed agencies’ documents on due diligence policies and procedures for identifying, assessing, and mitigating foreign ownership and employee affiliations risks. GAO interviewed program officials from the Small Business Administration, and participating agencies’ SBIR and STTR program offices, research security offices, and counterintelligence offices. To determine the extent to which agencies collect or track data on efforts to manage foreign risks, GAO obtained and analyzed the agencies’ documents and data from FY2024 and FY2025 on both risk areas.
For more information, contact Candice N. Wright at WrightC@gao.gov.
